blocks.block_content: A Priori Integral Persistent Excitation in Conservative Polynomial ODEs with Higher-Order Interactions
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: Aleksandr Semenov ∗
blocks.label: Text

blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: Abstract
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: The paper proposes an approach for verifying integral persistent excitation, which is im- portant in problems of parameter identification and adaptive control in nonlinear dynamical systems. The approach works for conservative polynomial ODEs a priori without knowledge of the parameters. Rigorous proofs of the corresponding theorems are provided. An example of a nonlinear dynamical system with higher-order interactions and the application of the pro- posed method to it are analyzed. The proof of the main result is formalized in the Lean formal verification language.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: Keywords: persistent excitation, complex systems, parameters estimation, three-wave interactions
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: 1 Introduction
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: arXiv:2607.00091v1 [math.OC] 30 Jun 2026
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: In physical problems, as well as in problems of chemistry, mechanics, biology, and economics, it is necessary to estimate parameters of dynamical systems [1]. This is precisely the main question of parametric identification theory. Nevertheless, parameter estimation algorithms are often invented outside the cybernetics journals, for example, in physics papers [2, 3], whenever a corresponding need arises.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: Besides inventing a method for parameter estimation, it is important to be certain that the obtained estimates are accurate and correct. The performance criterion for identification algorithms is usually the persistent excitation (PE) condition and its various modifications: weak PE, interval excitation, etc. [4–7].
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: However, a paradox arises here. First, the PE condition is not easy to prove even for known parameter values, because one needs to verify an inequality for the integral of a function along the trajectory. Second, verifying the PE condition is of interest before the parameters are identified; consequently, one has to work with a system where the parameters are unknown. Coping with these difficulties is hard, and often even in very strong papers the PE condition is introduced as an assumption [8–10] or the question of identifiability is not raised [2]. A priori ways to verify the PE condition are poorly developed [11], and publications on this topic are rare [11–13]. The aim of the present paper is to propose a method to solve these problems for a certain class of systems.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: When identifying parameters of complex autonomous nonlinear systems with higher-order inter- actions, the question becomes especially acute. In classical approaches, PE is often provided by an input signal (for instance, a sum of sinusoids is fed into the input); however, for a complex system

blocks.block_content: such an intervention may be too crude, especially since the influence of external inputs on systems with higher-order interactions cannot be considered completely understood [14]. For example, for ecological systems such an approach would mean regular mass culling of animals alternating with their abundant feeding.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: In the present paper, we restrict ourselves to conservative dynamical systems governed by poly- nomial ODEs. Furthermore, for simplicity and clarity of exposition (similarly to [11]) we will consider the PE condition for the state variable vector.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces affine integral excitation and its scalar form. Section 3 formulates the problem setting for a polynomial vector field on a compact invariant set. Section 4 presents the main result on the absence of sticking to hyperplanes and affine IPE. Sections 5 and 5.1 consider a resonant triad model and the application of the main theorem to it. Section 6 Concludes the article and is devoted to the development of work ideas. The proof of the main theorem is deferred to the appendix.

blocks.block_content: 6 Conclusion
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: In this paper we have proposed an approach for verifying integral persistent excitation for conser- vative polynomial ODEs a priori , without knowledge of the parameters. Rigorous proofs of the corresponding statements are provided. Using the three-wave interaction model as an example, we have shown how the method can be applied to systems with higher-order interactions. The reason- ing given for the illustrative example can be repeated without much difficulty for substantially more complex models, such as resonant cascades. The authors hope that the community will find these results interesting and will use them for their own models. Future research will be aimed at ap- plying the approach to various concrete problems of identification and adaptive control of complex systems, as well as at extending the results to the case of systems with dissipation.

blocks.block_content: Remark 1 (Important remarks on Lemmas 9 and 10) . 1. The estimate in Lemma \ref{lem:sep} is uniform over all $x_0\in K\setminus W_\delta$ and all unit normals $a$.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: 2. In Lemma \ref{lem:exit} it is important only that at the initial moment $x_0\notin W_\delta$; the subsequent dynamics may enter $W_\delta$ and leave it many times.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: 3. The number $T_*$ can be chosen arbitrarily small and then adjusted to other estimates.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: Estimate of the number of intersections with surfaces
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: To obtain an estimate of the average time, one must exclude the situation where the trajectory frequently leaves and immediately enters $U_\eps(H)$. Therefore it is important to bound from above the number of intersections with the boundaries $\{l=\pm\eps\}$ on each time block. The Novikov–Yakovenko theorem is used for this purpose.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: Proposition 11 (Novikov–Yakovenko theorem, autonomous case) . Let a polynomial ODE
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: \dot{x}=p(x), \qquad x \in \mathbb{R}^n,
blocks.label: Formula

blocks.block_content: be given, where the $p_i(x)$ have degree at most $d$. Assume that the absolute values of the coefficients of these polynomials are bounded by $r$.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: Let $\Gamma: I \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be a trajectory on an interval $I \subset \mathbb{R}$ that is contained in a ball of radius $r$. The length of the interval $I$ also does not exceed $r$.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: Lemma 12 (Uniform bound on intersections) . For a fixed $T_0$ and small $\delta,\eps$ there exists a universal constant $N$ such that for any hyperplane $H$ the number of intersections of the trajectory with the surfaces $\{l=\pm\eps\}$ on any interval of length $T_0$ does not exceed $N$.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: Proof. First fix a hyperplane $H$. Consider the two surfaces given by the linear polynomials $l(x)\pm\eps$. Since $K$ is compact, $\eps$ is small, and the hyperplane $H$ intersects the compact set $K$, the coefficients of all these polynomials are bounded by a constant that does not depend on the concrete small values of $\delta$ and $\eps$. By the Novikov–Yakovenko theorem \ref{prop:novikov_yakovenko}, the number of zeros of each of these polynomials along the trajectory on an interval of length $T_0$ is bounded by some constant $N$.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: It remains to observe that choosing another hyperplane changes nothing essential: the Novikov–Yakovenko theorem is insensitive to such a transition — its estimate depends on the degree of the polynomials and the dimension of the space, and on the compact set the coefficients of the corresponding linear polynomials remain uniformly bounded after normalization.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: Appendix D Proof of the Main Theorem
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: First we use the set $X_0$ from Proposition \ref{prop:step0_X0_2}. Take arbitrary $x\in X_0$ and an affine hyperplane $H=\{l=0\}$.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: We prove by contradiction. Assume that for the chosen $x\in X_0$ and $H$ the fraction of time in $U_\eps(H)$ does not tend to zero as $\eps\to0$. For a chosen small $\delta$ we partition time into blocks. In each block the time in $U_\eps(H)$ is split into two parts:
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content:
\text{(i) inside }W_\delta,
    \qquad
    \text{(ii) outside }W_\delta.
blocks.label: Formula

blocks.block_content: For the first part we already have a small average estimate from Step 0. For the second part we need to show that for sufficiently small $\eps$ the average time outside $W_\delta$ can also be made arbitrarily small.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: Step 1: choice of δ . Assume the contrary: there exist $\gamma>0$ and a sequence $\eps_k\to0$ such that
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: \limsup_{T\to\infty}\frac1T\int_0^T\mathbf 1_{U_{\eps_k}(H)}(\Phi^t x)\dd t\ge\gamma.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: By the definition of $X_0$ we can choose $\delta>0$ so that
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: b_\delta(x)=\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac1T\int_0^T\mathbf 1_{W_\delta}(\Phi^t x)\dd t<\frac{\gamma^2}{64}.
blocks.label: Formula

blocks.block_content: For this $\delta$ we further fix the exit time estimate from Lemma \ref{lem:exit} and the constant $c_\delta$ from Lemma \ref{lem:sep}.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: Step 2: blocks and bad blocks. Choose the block length $T_0=1$. Consider a large time $T=mT_0$. The number $T$ is chosen large enough so that the average
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: \frac1T\int_0^T\mathbf 1_{W_\delta}(\Phi^t x)\dd t
blocks.label: Formula

blocks.block_content: is sufficiently close to its limit from \eqref{eq:small_W_delta_2}. Partition $[0,mT_0]$ into blocks
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content:
I_j=[(j-1)T_0,jT_0],
    \qquad j=1,\dots,m.
blocks.label: Formula

blocks.block_content: Denote the fraction of time in $W_\delta$ inside a block by
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: v_j=\frac1{T_0}\int_{I_j}\mathbf 1_{W_\delta}(\Phi^t x)\dd t,
blocks.label: Formula

blocks.block_content: and the fraction of time in $U_\eps(H)$ by
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: w_j=\frac1{T_0}\int_{I_j}\mathbf 1_{U_\eps(H)}(\Phi^t x)\dd t.
blocks.label: Formula

blocks.block_content: We call a block $I_j$ bad if $v_j\ge\gamma/8$.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: Since $x\in X_0$, for the chosen $\delta$ we have
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: \lim_{m\to\infty}\frac1m\sum_{j=1}^m v_j<\frac{\gamma^2}{64}.
blocks.label: Formula

blocks.block_content: Hence, for all sufficiently large $m$ ,
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: \frac1m\sum_{j=1}^m v_j<\frac{\gamma^2}{64}.
blocks.label: Formula

blocks.block_content: If $m_{\mathrm{bad}}$ is the number of bad blocks, then
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content:
\frac{m_{\mathrm{bad}}}{m}\cdot\frac\gamma8
    \le\frac1m\sum_{j=1}^m v_j
    <\frac{\gamma^2}{64},
    \qquad
    \frac{m_{\mathrm{bad}}}{m}<\frac\gamma8.
blocks.label: Formula

blocks.block_content: Step 3: fixing the time grid and the number of intersections N . By the Novikov–Yakovenko theorem and Lemma \ref12: for the chosen $T_0$ and sufficiently small $\eps$ there exists a universal constant $N$ such that on each block of length $T_0$ the number of intersections of the trajectory with the surfaces $\{l=\pm\eps\}$ does not exceed $N$.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: Consequently, the number of entries into $U_\eps(H)$ on one block is at most $N/2$. Here an entry into $U_\eps(H)$ means the initial moment of each continuous interval of stay in $U_\eps(H)$.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: Choose $T_*>0$ so small that
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: \frac{N}{2}T_*<\frac\gamma8.
blocks.label: Formula

blocks.block_content: This is possible because $T_*$ in Lemma \ref{lem:exit} can be taken arbitrarily small. Next fix $\eps\le\eps_*(\delta)$ so that the bound on the number of intersections and the exit time estimate are applicable.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: More precisely, the order of choice is as follows: first pick a small range for $\eps$, then obtain the corresponding estimate $N$ from the Novikov–Yakovenko theorem, then choose $T_*$ so that 18 holds, and then, if necessary, decrease the admissible $\eps$ according to Lemma 10. The estimate $N$ does not increase from such a decrease.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: Step 5: good block, case 1. Consider a good block, i.e., a block for which $v_j<\gamma/8$. Consider the next entry into $U_\eps(H)$.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: First case: the entry occurs outside $W_\delta$. At the moment of entry $x_0\notin W_\delta$, hence by Lemma10 the trajectory leaves $U_\eps(H)$ in time at most $T_*$. It does not matter whether it later enters $W_\delta$ during this interval or not: Lemma 10 gives the answer independently of a subsequent entry into $W_\delta$.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: Step 6: good block, case 2. Second case: the entry occurs inside $W_\delta$. Let the trajectory first stay in $W_\delta$ for time $\tau_i$, then leave $W_\delta$ and, as in the first case, leave $U_\eps(H)$ in time at most $T_*$. Therefore for each such entry we obtain a contribution not exceeding $\tau_i+T_*$.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: \sum_i(\tau_i+T_*).
blocks.label: Formula

blocks.block_content: There are at most $N/2$ entries, so the contribution of the parts after leaving $W_\delta$ does not exceed $(N/2)T_*$. On a good block the sum of all times $\tau_i$ spent inside $W_\delta$ does not exceed $\gamma/8$. Hence,
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: w_j\le\frac\gamma8+\frac{N}{2}T_*\le\frac\gamma4.
blocks.label: Formula

blocks.block_content: Preventing fast oscillation. To estimate the total time in $U_\eps(H)$ via the number of entries, one must exclude too frequent entries and exits. This is precisely why Lemma 12 is used: the number of intersections with the boundaries $\{l=\pm\eps\}$ on each block is bounded above, so the trajectory cannot oscillate arbitrarily many times between the boundaries.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: Step 7: final assembly. For good blocks we obtain $w_j\le\gamma/4$; for bad blocks we use the crude bound $w_j\le1$. Then by (17)
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content:
\frac1m\sum_{j=1}^m w_j
    \le\frac{m-m_{\mathrm{bad}}}{m}\cdot\frac\gamma4
    +\frac{m_{\mathrm{bad}}}{m}\cdot1
    <\frac\gamma4+\frac\gamma8
    =\frac{3\gamma}{8}.
blocks.label: Formula

blocks.block_content: Thus the fraction of time spent in $U_\eps(H)$ does not exceed $3\gamma/8$. This contradicts the assumption \eqref15. Consequently, the fraction of time in $U_\eps(H)$ tends to zero as $\eps\to0$, i.e., 5 is proved.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: It remains to deduce affine IPE. If the scalar estimate \eqref{eq:ipe_scalar_2} does not hold, then there exist $T_j\to\infty$ and normalized pairs $(a_j,b_j)$, $\|a_j\|^2+b_j^2=1$, such that
blocks.label: Text

blocks.block_content: \frac1{T_j}\int_0^{T_j}|a_j\cdot \Phi^t(x)+b_j|^2\dd t\to0.
blocks.label: Formula

blocks.block_content: Passing to a subsequence, we assume $(a_j,b_j)\to(a,b)$. If $a=0$, then $|b|=1$, which is impossible. If $a\ne0$, then for the hyperplane $H=\{y:a\cdot y+b=0\}$ property \eqref{eq:main_nonsticking_2} gives a small average fraction of time in $U_\eta(H)$ for sufficiently small $\eta>0$, while outside this neighborhood $|a\cdot \Phi^t(x)+b|\ge \|a\|\eta$. This yields a positive lower bound for the limit inferior of the mean square, a contradiction. Hence 2, and therefore 6, holds.
blocks.label: Text
